input: Write a short story for a literary magazine submission

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Literary magazines have strict word count ranges (flash fiction ~1000 words vs. short story ~5000-7500 words); this determines the depth of plot, character, and structure possible.
Genre and tone (literary realism, magical realism, horror, speculative, etc.) fundamentally shape every creative decision from voice to imagery to plot mechanics.
Whether the user has a specific magazine in mind changes everything — that publication's aesthetic, submission guidelines, and audience should directly influence the story's style and content.
Knowing who the protagonist is (age, background, situation) anchors the story's perspective and emotional core, which is the starting point of any plot.
Submission deadlines determine urgency and how many drafting/revision cycles are realistic, which shapes the planning timeline.
The user's definition of done — a polished final draft, just a first draft to workshop, or a full submission packet with cover letter — determines how far the plan needs to go.
Knowing whether the user has a story idea already or needs one from scratch determines the very first action step and how much creative development work is needed.

gold.taskTitle: Write a Short Story for Literary Magazine
gold.taskDescription: Write an original short story polished enough to submit to a literary magazine for publication consideration.

questions.title: What word count are you aiming for?
questions.description: Determine the target length — flash fiction (under 1,000 words), short story (1,000–5,000), or longer — since this defines the scope of plot and character development possible.

questions.title: What genre or tone should the story have?
questions.description: Identify the desired genre (literary realism, magical realism, speculative, horror, etc.) and tone (dark, hopeful, sardonic), as these shape every creative decision.

questions.title: Do you have a specific magazine in mind to submit to?
questions.description: A named publication (e.g., The Sun, One Story, Ploughshares) brings concrete submission guidelines and a known editorial aesthetic that should directly influence the story.

questions.title: Do you already have a story idea or premise?
questions.description: Establish whether the user is starting from a blank page or has a character, conflict, or concept in mind, as this determines the very first step of the plan.

questions.title: Who is the central character of the story?
questions.description: Capture key details about the protagonist — their situation, identity, or struggle — to anchor the emotional core and narrative perspective.

questions.title: Is there a submission deadline you are working toward?
questions.description: A specific deadline (or open-ended timeline) determines how many drafting and revision cycles are realistic and how urgently the plan needs to move.

questions.title: What does a successful outcome look like to you?
questions.description: Clarify whether the goal is a polished submission-ready draft, a first draft to workshop with peers, or a complete submission packet including a cover letter.
